arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_north_d3_038 is an anonymous reconstructed roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: NO SEPARATE WORKPLACE. A carpenter in this town worked in other people's buildings, in the street, or in the dwelling itself, and inventing a shop for the sake of a link would be inventing a building.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: Baptiste Chevalier

occupation.note: THE TRADE THE TOWN NEEDED MOST AND THE ONE THE DOCUMENTED LAYER UNDER-COUNTS WORST. The 1835 town census counts 3,265 people in 398 dwellings; Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 describes a settlement of a few dozen buildings, and the reconstruction specification puts 665 roofs on the ground by July 1835. Several hundred of those roofs went up inside eighteen months. Even at a crew of three raising a one-room frame cottage in three weeks, that is on the order of forty carpenter-years of work in a year and a half. Andreas names four carpenters and one ship carpenter in the whole of the 1833 town. Ten carpenter households are inferred against the schedule's eight W2 carpenter-or-joiner shops, because a house carpenter worked on the frame in the street and not in a shop: the shop count is a floor under the trade, not a measure of it. ONE FURTHER CARPENTER HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-14, AND THE ROOF IS THE REASON RATHER THAN A NEW FINDING ABOUT THE TRADE. The count above is stated as a floor in its own last clause, and what held it at ten was method rule 5: every household must be housed, and housing one where no anonymous roof of the right family and district stands means raising an invented building. The block parcel at Randolph and Wells has since put a D3 one-room frame cottage on the plat in the South Division - a roof the 665-roof programme had already counted, in the family this layer houses nine of its ten carpenters in. Adopting it raises no building, invents no position and moves no other record; it puts an argued occupant under a roof that was standing anonymously. Eleven carpenter households are inferred, still against eight W2 shops and still a floor. ONE FURTHER CARPENTER HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-14, ON THE SAME TERMS AND UNDER A RULE THAT NOW HAS THREE TESTS RATHER THAN TWO. The count is still a floor by its own text and still stated against eight W2 shops. The block parcel at Randolph and Market has put a second D3 one-room frame cottage on the plat in the South Division - a roof the 665-roof programme had already counted, in the family this layer houses ten of its eleven carpenters in, and in the division it houses five of them in. The third test is the one T-A4 applied by hand when it refused this trade a roof west of the river; here it passes rather than being waived, which is the difference. Twelve carpenter households are inferred. Adopting the roof raises no building, invents no position and moves no other record. ONE FURTHER CARPENTER HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AND UNDER THE SAME THREE TESTS. The count is still a floor by its own text and still stated against eight W2 shops. The block parcel at South Water and Franklin has put a third D3 one-room frame cottage on the plat in the South Division - a roof the 665-roof programme had already counted, in the family this layer houses eleven of its twelve carpenters in, and in the division it houses six of them in. Thirteen carpenter households are inferred. Adopting the roof raises no building, invents no position and moves no other record. WHAT IS NEW HERE IS THE FRONTAGE, AND IT DOES NOT CHANGE THE ANSWER: this is the first block roof adopted on South Water Street, the town's business front, rather than one street back from it. Rule 6 asks about the trade's family and the trade's division and says nothing about which street a roof stands on, deliberately - the roof is a dwelling either way, and a carpenter living on the busiest street in town is not a claim this layer has to argue, because the 665-roof programme already put a dwelling there and the adoption changes only who is under it.

name_basis.value: invented from the French colonial and metis of the Detroit and Milwaukee country pool
name_basis.note: THE NAME IS INVENTED. No source names this resident, and this field is not a finding about anybody — it is a label so that a reconstructed household reads as a household rather than as a row in a table. It was drawn from the French colonial and metis of the Detroit and Milwaukee country pool in data/reconstruction/1835_invented_name_pools.json, which is seeded from the names of the 76 ATTESTED residents this project holds — real people, named from cited sources — so that an invented resident is named the way this town's documented residents were actually named rather than the way a story would name one. The community was drawn WITHOUT a weighting that any source supports. The proportions of the documented layer, which is overwhelmingly New England and New York with an older French colonial presence and a small Irish one. Applied to every trade for which no source speaks to who did the work. The evidence for the pool itself: The oldest continuously present community in this dataset and among the best attested. Beaubien appears three times among the named residents; recorded origins include 'Detroit and the Milwaukee trade, of a French colonial family', 'a French-descended trading family of the Detroit and Milwaukee country', and 'Detroit; his father an Irish officer in the British army, his mother Potawatomi'. The river and lake carrying trade of this place was worked by this community, which is why the boatman weighting below cites evidence rather than asserting a guess.

THE WEIGHTING TOWARD LABOURING TRADES IS ITSELF AN INFERENCE and is marked as such wherever it is applied: the Illinois and Michigan Canal contracts were not let until 1836, so the large Irish labouring population of the later 1830s is arriving around and after the scene date rather than established by it. What the pool claims is that Irish names belong in this town on 1 July 1835, which the documented layer supports; it does not claim any particular trade was Irish.
